title: Senate wraps up budget debates; bloodbath looms
summary: The Senate wrapped up yesterday its marathon plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion budget after five days, marked by the shortest interpellation period in Senate history, according to…

blocks.text: November 29, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate wrapped up yesterday its marathon plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion budget after five days, marked by the shortest interpellation period in Senate history, according to Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian.
Senators met the target of finishing floor interpellations during the weekend, capping a week of sessions where major projects of the Marcos administration were closely scrutinized.
Gatchalian adjourned the session at 1:24 a.m. and scheduled the resumption for the period of amendments on Dec. 4. He said swift pace of the session did not diminish the quality of debates.
Speaking to dwIZ yesterday, Gatchalian confirmed that he was in his office over the weekend to discuss with Senate finance committee chairman Sen. JV Ejercito the next steps for the spending measure.

“The budget needs to get done... Every hour, every day counts,” he said. Asked if the five-day stretch was historically the shortest period of budget interpellations, Gatchalian replied: “Yes, this is the shortest. Before there was six days.”
The senate president stressed that the pace did not diminish the chamber’s review of agency budgets, noting that senators worked through meal breaks to finish on schedule.
Once session resumes, the Senate will open the period of amendments before voting to approve its version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill on second and third reading.

Designated Senate conferees will then meet with their House counterparts in the bicameral conference committee to reconcile clashing provisions, with the leadership targeting ratification before Dec. 17 to avoid a reenacted budget.
‘Real bloodbath’

After the Senate stripped P99.3 billion in House-inserted local projects from the Department of Public Works and Highways’ proposed budget, Senators are expecting a “real bloodbath” in the upcoming bicameral conference committee.

During his interpellation of the DPWH budget yesterday, Sen. Panfilo Lacson said while the Senate finance committee has already cut local projects to restore funding for foreign-assisted and flagship infrastructure projects, senators still have work to do to clean up their own committee report before facing House counterparts.
Lacson said this was because the Senate’s own version still has P38.5 billion in undocumented projects and P41 billion in vaguely labeled multi-purpose buildings (MPBs).
“I think the real bloodbath will be in the bicam conference. And I just hope the agencies will support us when it gets to the bicam,” he said.
Citing findings passed to him by the People’s Budget Coalition, Lacson flagged 1,094 projects worth P38.5 billion under the Senate version that lack supporting documents.
He also questioned 2,806 MPB line items worth P41 billion in the Senate version that fail to specify what structures are actually being built.

“If it’s a public market, call it a public market. If it’s a sports complex, call it a sports complex. Just don’t call it a ‘multi-purpose building,’ period,” Lacson added, recounting how his staff struggled to track down a supposed MPB in Zambales which turned out to be a public market with another unidentified structure rising at the same compound.
Lacson also pointed out that government construction has contracted for six quarters, averaging negative 29 percent from January to September 2026.
The numbers represent a 31.5 percent drop in the first quarter, 33.4 percent in the second and 15.1 percent in the third.
He traced the drop to the cut in the DPWH budget from P1.09 trillion in 2025 to P529 billion in 2026, after what he called the “trauma of flood control anomalies.”
“This is what brought our gross domestic product (GDP) down to 2.1 percent. This is one of the primary reasons why our economic growth is so low,” he said.
Ejercito said hitting the growth target requires P1.3 trillion in infrastructure spending, or about P300 billion per quarter.

Lacson cited Development Budget Coordination Committee estimates showing that a 3.5-percent GDP target requires 6.7-percent growth from the fourth quarter his year into the first quarter of 2027. Reaching five percent requires 11.7-percent growth, which he called a “tall order.”
He also questioned P3.06 billion – or P180 million per region – for evacuation centers in the 2027 DPWH budget that lacked locations.
Lacson noted that regional lump sums also appeared in the 2025 budget at P100 million per region and in the 2026 budget at P75 million per region.
He compared the P180-million figure with the Office of Civil Defense’s (OCD) P75-million construction cost.

“My point… is perhaps we could hold off on this for now – or deduct it for now – and instead, realign the P180 million per region for 2027, pending the identification of the P100 million per region in 2025 and the P75 million per region in 2026,” Lacson said.
Ejercito said the P180 million covers two evacuation centers at P90 million each under the Ligtas Pinoy Center Act, which requires a 3,000-square-meter lot and a 530-person capacity.
Scholarships at risk
Meanwhile, more than 187,600 college students risk losing their scholarships next year due to budget cuts made by the House of Representatives in the government’s 2027 higher education budget.

During the Senate plenary debates on the budgets of the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) and State Universities and Colleges (SUCs), budget sponsor Sen. Joel Villanueva confirmed that roughly P15 billion was slashed from CHED’s requested allocation.
CHED’s proposed budget was at P38.82 billion, while SUCs’ were at P138.3 billion under the Senate version.
Pressed by Sen. Bam Aquino on whether the cuts put 187,600 students at risk of losing their Tertiary Education Subsidies (TES), Villanueva said it could be more than that.

Both senators warned that cutting off subsidies for current scholars after a year of support would force students out of school, even with free tuition under Republic Act 10931, as families continue to struggle with rising food and transportation costs.

Aquino stressed that the Philippines’ 66 percent tertiary completion rate is the highest in ASEAN, a rare “bright spot” in the country’s education metrics that he credited to free college and additional student subsidies.

To prevent mass dropouts and fund the new law, Aquino said his office – along with the offices of Villanueva, Gatchalian and Lacson – is working to source roughly P5.5 billion to cover both the continuing TES grants and the Presidential Merit Scholarship Program.

In a statement, the Alliance of Health Workers (AHW) lamented that the Philippine General Hospital faces a P805.457-million budget cut, while public hospitals under the Department of Health are subjects of a combined reduction of P11.075 billion, excluding the P5.441-billion cuts in specialty hospitals, while P409.406 million will be slashed from the personal services budget intended for health workers’ salaries and benefits.

“Instead of cutting hospital funds and personnel services, the government must increase health workers’ entry-level salaries to P36,000 for Salary Grade 1 health workers and government employees, and P50,000 for nurses and allied health professionals,” the group said during the Senate deliberations on the proposed 2027 health budget on Friday. — Rhodina Villanueva
